We need retrosynthesis route up to 3 steps, leaves commercially available, total price <=9999. Need propose route using templates. We have some candidate templates from search. Need to construct route JSON.

We need to break target into simpler precursors. The target: Cc1ccc(NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2)cc1. Contains a tolyl sulfonamide attached to a phenyl with a trans-α,β-unsaturated amide attached to an aniline (para-aminobenzamide). So possible disconnections: sulfonamide formation (S-N bond) between sulfonyl chloride and aniline. Also amide formation between acid chloride and aniline. Also maybe Wittig for C=C.

Goal: 3 steps max. Could do: Step1: sulfonyl chloride (p-tolylsulfonyl chloride) + aniline derivative (the other phenyl with side chain) to form sulfonamide. Step2: amide formation between acryloyl chloride (or similar) and aniline (3-aminobenzamide). Actually the side chain is /C=C/C(=O)N-Ph-NH2? Wait structure: ...c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2. So phenyl ring (ring B) attached to sulfonamide, and on that phenyl there is a para substituent: a trans-α,β-unsaturated amide attached to an aniline (para-aminobenzamide). So we could disconnect the C=C double bond via a Heck coupling? Or via a Wittig from aldehyde? Simpler: use a Knoevenagel condensation between benzaldehyde (with amide) and acetaldehyde? But we need trans geometry.

Maybe easier: use a Suzuki coupling to install the phenyl with side chain onto the sulfonyl phenyl? But we need to keep sulfonamide.

Alternative: Build the whole molecule via two disconnections: (1) sulfonamide formation, (2) amide formation, (3) C=C formation via Wittig or Horner-Wadsworth-Emmons.

Thus 3 steps.

Precursors needed: (A) p-tolylsulfonyl chloride (commercial). (B) 4-aminophenyl with side chain: maybe 4-(2-formyl)aniline? Actually we need after amide formation and C=C formation produce the side chain. Let's design route:

Target T.

Retrosynthetic step 1: Break sulfonamide S-N bond. Precursors: p-tolylsulfonyl chloride (ClSO2C6H4CH3) and aniline derivative (4-(E)-3-(4-aminophenyl)acrylamide? Wait the sulfonamide attaches to an aniline (the phenyl B) at its para position? Actually the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to phenyl B (c2ccc(... )cc2). So the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to phenyl B as -NH- linking to sulfonyl group. So the sulfonamide precursor is the aniline (phenyl B) with NH2 (para to side chain). So we need 4-aminophenyl with side chain (the side chain is attached to the same phenyl B at para? Actually the side chain is attached to phenyl B at para position relative to sulfonamide? The SMILES: c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2. The sulfonamide attaches to the phenyl B via N (NS(=O)(=O)c2...). So the phenyl B has two substituents: sulfonamide at one position (maybe para) and the side chain at another (maybe para). In SMILES, c2ccc(... )cc2 indicates substitution at position 1 (connected to sulfonyl) and at position 4 (the /C=C...). So they are para to each other.

Thus the aniline precursor after sulfonamide formation will be phenyl B bearing NH2 (the sulfonamide nitrogen) and the side chain attached (still). Actually after sulfonamide formation, the nitrogen becomes part of sulfonamide, not free NH2. So the precursor before step1 is phenyl B with an NH2 (as sulfonamide nitrogen) and the side chain attached (still). So we need a phenyl B with an NH2 (para to side chain). That is 4-(E)-3-(4-aminophenyl)acrylamide? Wait the side chain includes an amide attached to an aniline (c3ccccc3N). So the side chain is -CH=CH-C(=O)-NH-Ph-NH2. So the phenyl B attaches to the carbonyl side chain via the double bond. So the phenyl B is attached to the alkene carbon (beta carbon). So the side chain is attached to phenyl B via the alkene.

Thus the phenyl B precursor after sulfonamide formation still has the side chain (alkene + amide). So we need to construct that side chain earlier.

Thus step2: break amide C-N bond. Precursors: acryloyl chloride (or acryloyl bromide) and aniline (c3ccccc3N). Actually the amide is between carbonyl and aniline (c3ccccc3N). So we can form amide via coupling of acryloyl chloride with aniline (para-aminobenzene). So precursor: acryloyl chloride (CH2=CH-COCl) and 4-aminobenzene (aniline). That's commercially available.

Step3: break C=C double bond. Could be formed via Wittig from aldehyde (4-(formyl)phenyl with side chain?) Actually we need the alkene connecting phenyl B to carbonyl. The alkene is trans between phenyl B and carbonyl carbon. Could be formed via Horner-Wadsworth-Emmons (HWE) from phosphonate and aldehyde. Simpler: use Heck coupling between phenyl B bromide and acrylate? But we already used acryloyl chloride for amide formation, which gives CH=CH-CO-... The double bond is already present in acryloyl chloride (CH2=CH-COCl). So after amide formation, we have CH2=CH-CO-NH-Ph-NH2. This is the side chain attached to phenyl B via the CH2=CH- (the double bond). Wait the double bond is between phenyl B and carbonyl carbon? Actually acryloyl chloride has CH2=CH-COCl. When we form amide, we get CH2=CH-CO-NH-Ph-NH2. The double bond is between CH2 and CH (the beta carbon). The phenyl B attaches to the CH2? In target, the double bond is /C=C/C(=O)N... The phenyl B attaches to the carbon of the double bond that is adjacent to carbonyl? Let's parse: /C=C/C(=O)N... The SMILES: /C=C/C(=O)N... Means phenyl B attached to the first carbon of the double bond (the one after slash). So phenyl B -CH=CH-CO-NH-Ph-NH2. So the double bond is between phenyl B carbon and CH (the beta carbon). In acryloyl chloride, the double bond is CH2=CH-COCl, where the carbonyl carbon is attached to CH (beta). To attach phenyl B to the CH2 side, we need to do a Heck coupling of phenyl B bromide with acryloyl chloride? Actually Heck couples aryl halide with alkene to form aryl-alkene bond. So we could start from phenyl B bromide (with NH2 protected maybe) and acryloyl chloride to form the aryl-alkene bond, then amide formation later. But we need amide after coupling.

Alternative route: Step1: Suzuki coupling of phenyl B bromide with vinyl boronic acid to give phenyl-CH=CH2, then oxidation to aldehyde, then Wittig with phosphonium ylide from aniline? Complex.

Given limited steps, maybe we can use a three-step route: (1) sulfonamide formation, (2) amide formation, (3) Heck coupling to install the alkene.

But Heck coupling would need aryl bromide (phenyl B with sulfonamide already attached) and acrylamide (CH2=CH-CO-NH-Ph-NH2). However the amide formation uses acryloyl chloride and aniline; that product is acryloyl anilide (CH2=CH-CO-NH-Ph-NH2). This can be used directly in Heck coupling as the alkene partner (it has terminal alkene). So step3: Heck coupling of phenyl B bromide (with sulfonamide) with acryloyl anilide to give the target.

Thus retrosynthesis: target -> break C-C bond formed in Heck (aryl-alkene). Precursors: (i) aryl bromide (p-tolyl sulfonyl phenyl bromide) and (ii) acryloyl anilide.

Now we need to ensure aryl bromide is commercially available. The aryl bromide is the phenyl B with sulfonamide attached? Actually after sulfonamide formation, the aryl bromide would have the sulfonamide already attached? Wait the sulfonamide formation attaches sulfonyl group to the aniline nitrogen, not to the aromatic carbon. The aryl bromide is the phenyl B with sulfonamide nitrogen attached (i.e., the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to phenyl B as -NH-SO2-Ph-tolyl). So the aryl bromide would be the phenyl B bearing the sulfonamide nitrogen (as -NH-SO2-Ph-tolyl) and a bromine at the position where the alkene will be attached (para to sulfonamide). So we need 4-bromo-2-(??) Actually the phenyl B has sulfonamide at position 1, bromine at position 4. So the precursor is 4-bromo-2-(??) Wait the sulfonamide attaches via nitrogen, not carbon. So the phenyl B is an aniline (NH2) that after sulfonamide formation becomes -NH-SO2-Ph-tolyl. So the aryl bromide is 4-bromo-2-(??) Actually the phenyl B is a phenyl ring with an NH (attached to sulfonyl) at position 1, and bromine at para position. So the compound is 4-bromo-2-(??) Not needed.

Is such brominated sulfonamide commercially available? Might be not. Could we reverse order: first do Heck coupling to attach phenyl B to acryloyl anilide, then sulfonamide formation? That would require phenyl B with NH2 (aniline) and bromine? Actually we could start with 4-bromo-2-methylaniline (p-bromo-toluidine) and sulfonyl chloride to form sulfonamide after Heck? But sulfonamide formation after Heck is okay because the sulfonamide nitrogen is free. So route: Step1: Heck coupling between 4-bromo-2-methylaniline (p-bromo-toluidine) and acryloyl anilide to give product with NH2 still free (attached to phenyl B). Then step2: sulfonyl chloride coupling to form sulfonamide. That is 2 steps total. But we also need amide formation earlier to get acryloyl anilide. So total 3 steps: (a) amide formation (acryloyl chloride + 4-aminobenzene) -> acryloyl anilide; (b) Heck coupling with 4-bromo-2-methylaniline -> intermediate with NH2; (c) sulfonyl chloride coupling with p-tolylsulfonyl chloride -> final product.

Check commercial availability: acryloyl chloride (ClC=CC(=O)Cl) is common. 4-aminobenzene (aniline) is common. 4-bromo-2-methylaniline (p-bromo-o-toluidine) is maybe commercially available. p-tolylsulfonyl chloride (tosyl chloride) is common.

Thus leaves: acryloyl chloride, aniline, 4-bromo-2-methylaniline, tosyl chloride. All cheap.

Now need to find templates for each step.

Step a: amide formation between acryloyl chloride and aniline. Template likely "acyl chloride + amine -> amide". Search for functional group formed: amide. Use search with functional_groups_formed ["amide"] and maybe bonds formed "C-N". Let's search.
